newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists kick off early election battle.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists kick off early election battle.

text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin launched a de facto electoral campaign a year early on Thursday with an appeal to other left-wing forces to forge a pact "to govern together".

"1997 will be a year of transition -- the Right will go from digestion of its victory to the fear of defeat," Jospin said, his sights set on "cohabitation", or power-sharing, with conservative Jacques Chirac after parliamentary elections due in early 1998.
The austere ex-education minister, who pushed Chirac to a surprisingly tight runoff in the 1995 presidential election, was speaking at a New Year reception for the press.
"The year is starting under poor auspices," Jospin went on. "The French are morose because the president has not fulfilled his promises and because they have been given nothing to look forward to."
He accused the centre-right government, plagued by internal rivalry, of giving in to orthodox economic thinking, becoming obsessed by privatisation and threatening the independence of the judiciary.
He also criticised it for clashing with Washington over African policy and over the NATO alliance.

His attacks were tempered, however, by a few kind words for Chirac. "The president's personal image is not bad...He has a kindly character," said Jospin, front-runner to serve as Chirac's prime minister if the Socialists win.

Jospin denied he was launching an electoral campaign this early, but pledged to forge a pact over the coming year with other leftist forces including Communists and Greens, and to build up a higher profile with rallies across the country.

"I am personally ready to study a pact on political orientation between left-wing parties and the environmentalists (with the aim of) governing together," Jospin said, adding that he wanted to forge an alternative parliamentary majority.

"We are ready to discuss European construction with other forces of the Left, but we will not yield to vetoes. We will not give up the single European currency," he said, a reference to objections from the Communists and the Greens.

At another New Year reception, Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary-general of Chirac's RPR party, said it would start talks next month with its junior coalition partner, the UDF, to draw up lists of joint candidates for the election.
From the summer onwards, Mancel said, the RPR and the UDF would draw up a common platform for government.

Jospin rejected charges that trade unions which led a series of protests and strikes in recent months had pushed his party out of the limelight, adding that the Socialists were ready to mobilise alongside unions if necessary to fight government plans to let private pensions funds operate.

The Socialist leader criticised Chirac for going back on the policy of his late mentor, General Charles de Gaulle, by restoring close French ties with the North Atlantic alliance despite making no mention in his election campaign of a warming of relations with NATO.

Asked which aspects of foreign policy, traditionally the preserve of the president, he would seek to change if named premier, Jospin answered: "Many aspects of the current foreign policy were laid down by (late Socialist president) Francois Mitterrand.

"So in many areas there is not necessarily opposition between the government and us (although) I think we will have to modify our African policy," said Jospin, who has urged a more critical stance towards autocratic African rulers.
